see about.verb type: action — dynamic; attending to something is a task you perform, and it takes the progressive freely: *she's seeing about a table for us*. Sense 2 (*we'll see about that*) is a fixed formula, not a free verb.
see about.passive: **no** — the prepositional passive is not idiomatic here: ✗ *a new passport was seen about*, ✗ *the leak has been seen about*. Use [see to](#see-to) when you need a passive.

see off.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: going to the gate to wave, and driving a rival away.
see off.passive: **yes** in both senses — *the recruits were seen off by the whole town*; *the challengers were seen off in straight sets*.

see out.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 1 is durative (you keep going until the clock runs out), sense 2 a single act of escorting.
see out.passive: **restricted** — natural in sense 2, *the visitors were seen out through the side entrance*; strained in sense 1, ✗ *her contract was seen out*.

see through.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1 and 2 (finishing a job, carrying someone along); sense 3 is a **stative** verb of perception and resists the progressive: ✗ *I'm seeing through him* — you say *I can see through him*.
see through.passive: **restricted** — good in sense 1, *the reforms were seen through over four years*, and with a thing in sense 3, *the excuse was seen through in about a second*. Sense 2 has none: ✗ *she was seen through the divorce by her humor*.

see to.verb type: action — dynamic; handling something to completion, and comfortable in the progressive: *who's seeing to the food?*
see to.passive: **yes** — one of the prepositional verbs that passivizes cleanly: *his hand was seen to before anyone asked a question*, *has the paperwork been seen to?* The frame *see to it that* has no passive.

seek out.verb type: action — dynamic; the deliberate effort is the whole meaning, and it takes the progressive: *she's seeking out the hardest route*.
seek out.passive: **yes**, and common in writing — *the families were sought out before the names were released*.

sell off.verb type: action — dynamic; a disposal carried out over a stretch of time: *the chain is selling off its stores*.
sell off.passive: **yes** — *everything that wasn't profitable was sold off after the merger*.

sell on.verb type: action — dynamic; persuasion is something you do to someone, and it takes the progressive: *he's still selling us on the neighborhood*.
sell on.passive: **yes**, and the participle is the commonest shape of all — *I was never really sold on the idea*.

sell out.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses; in sense 1 the participle has drifted toward an adjective of state, *the show is sold out* describing the condition rather than the event.
sell out.passive: **restricted** — sense 2 passivizes freely: *we were sold out by our own crew*. Senses 1 and 3 take no object and so have no passive; *the show sold out* is active despite the look of *sold out*.

sell out of.verb type: action — dynamic; a change of state reached through selling, usually reported as a completed fact: *they sold out of the blue ones by ten*.
sell out of.passive: **no** — the noun after *of* cannot be promoted: ✗ *croissants are sold out of by nine*. Say *the croissants sold out* instead.

sell short.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, though sense 1 usually reports a standing judgment: *people sell that town short until they visit*.
sell short.passive: **yes** — *she was sold short by everyone who interviewed her*; in finance, *the airline was sold short a week before the news broke*.

sell up.verb type: action — dynamic; a single decisive act, and intransitive: *after the second bad year he sold up*.
sell up.passive: **no** — intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *the business was sold up*.

send away.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; sense 2 is durative in effect (the person stays away for a stretch) but the verb itself names the act of dispatching.
send away.passive: **yes** — *the reporters at the gate were sent away*; *he was sent away to boarding school at eleven*.

send away for.verb type: action — dynamic; ordering by mail and then waiting, so it sits happily in the past: *I sent away for a catalog and forgot about it*.
send away for.passive: **no** — the three-part string blocks the prepositional passive: ✗ *a catalog was sent away for*, ✗ *the transcripts were sent away for in September*.

send back.verb type: action — dynamic; a single act of return, often instantaneous: *the steak was raw, so he sent it back*.
send back.passive: **yes** — *the shipment was sent back unopened*; *the form must be sent back with both signatures*.

send down.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses — a demotion, an expulsion, a sentence.
send down.passive: **yes**, and the passive is the usual shape — *he was sent down to Triple-A in June*, *he was sent down from Oxford in his second year*, *he got sent down for fraud*.

send for.verb type: action — dynamic; summoning someone, and urgent by nature: *when the fever spiked, we sent for help*.
send for.passive: **yes** — one of the few prepositional verbs whose passive is fully idiomatic: *a doctor was sent for immediately*, *she was sent for in the middle of the night*.

send in.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: submitting paperwork, and ordering people into a place.
send in.passive: **yes** — *your application must be sent in before the first*; *the National Guard was sent in that night*.

send off.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 1 carries a note of finality once the thing leaves your hands.
send off.passive: **yes** — *the check was sent off this morning*; sense 3 lives almost entirely in the passive, *he was sent off in the seventieth minute*.

send out.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; sense 2 (radiate heat, light, a signal) describes an ongoing process and takes the progressive naturally: *the beacon is sending out a pulse every four seconds*.
send out.passive: **yes** — *the invitations were sent out in March*; *a pulse is sent out every four seconds*. Sense 2 with a plain source is stilted in the passive: ✗ *more heat is sent out by that little stove*.

send out for.verb type: action — dynamic; ordering food to be brought to you, and habitual in the present: *they send out for Thai every Friday*.
send out for.passive: **no** — the three-part string admits no passive: ✗ *pizza was sent out for*, ✗ *coffee was sent out for at two in the morning*.

send up.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: imprisoning someone, and parodying them.
send up.passive: **yes** — *he got sent up on a tax charge*; *local news anchors are sent up on the show every week*.

set about.verb type: action — dynamic, and inceptive — it names the beginning of a task, which is why it takes an *-ing* complement: *she set about cleaning the garage*.
set about.passive: **no** in American use — the *-ing* clause cannot be promoted: ✗ *cleaning the garage was set about*. Only the British 'attack' sense passivizes: *he was set about in the parking lot*.

set apart.verb type: action in form but **stative** in meaning — it states a standing difference rather than an event, and resists the progressive: ✗ *patience is setting the best teachers apart*.
set apart.passive: **yes**, though far less common than the active *what sets her apart* — *she is set apart by her patience*, *the two paintings are set apart by one small detail*.

set aside.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: saving something, shelving a question, annulling a judgment.
set aside.passive: **yes** — *two hours were set aside for the call*; *the verdict was set aside by an appeals court in March*.

set back.verb type: action — dynamic in sense 1 (a delay is something that happens to progress); sense 2 (cost money) is **stative**, a *cost*-type verb, and rejects the progressive: ✗ *that watch is setting him back a thousand dollars*.
set back.passive: **restricted** — sense 1 passivizes: *the schedule was set back a month by the storm*. Sense 2 behaves like *cost* and refuses it: ✗ *a thousand dollars was set him back*, ✗ *he was set back a thousand dollars by that watch*.

set down.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: lowering something, recording it, landing an aircraft.
set down.passive: **yes** — *the rules were set down in 1912 and never revised*; *the helicopter was set down in a parking lot*.

set forth.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 1 is a formal act of statement, sense 2 a departure.
set forth.passive: **yes** in sense 1, and that is where the phrase usually lives — *the conditions are set forth in section four*. Sense 2 takes no object: ✗ *first light was set forth at*.

set in.verb type: action — dynamic and inceptive: it names the onset of a condition that then persists. Intransitive, and the progressive is odd: ✗ *the rain is setting in* is possible but rare beside *the rain set in*.
set in.passive: **no** — intransitive, so no passive exists: ✗ *panic was set in*, ✗ *the rain was set in around noon*.

set off.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: departing, triggering, and heightening by contrast (sense 3 reports a standing effect: *the dark frame sets off the painting*).
set off.passive: **restricted** — senses 2 and 3 passivize freely: *the smoke alarm was set off by burnt toast*, *the painting is set off by the dark frame*. Sense 1 has no object and no passive: ✗ *the coast was set off for*.

set out.verb type: action — dynamic throughout; sense 2 (*set out to do*) states an intention held from the start and appears mostly in the past: *he never set out to be famous*.
set out.passive: **restricted** — sense 3 passivizes and often prefers it: *the risks are set out in plain language*, *the tools were set out in order of size*. Senses 1 and 2 take no object: ✗ *sunrise was set out before*.

set to.verb type: action — dynamic and inceptive: starting in on work or food with energy, and often an imperative: *set to, everyone*.
set to.passive: **no** — intransitive, so nothing can be promoted: ✗ *the dishes were set to*.

set up.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: founding, assembling, arranging, framing.
set up.passive: **yes**, and heavily used — *the company was set up in a garage*; *a call has been set up for Thursday*; sense 4 is passive by default, *I was set up*.

set upon.verb type: action — dynamic; a sudden attack, and punctual rather than durative.
set upon.passive: **yes**, and the passive is where the phrase actually lives — *he was set upon by three men outside the station*, *the hikers were set upon by a pack of dogs*.

shake down.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: extorting, searching, and giving something a trial run.
shake down.passive: **yes** — *every shop on the block was shaken down for protection money*; *the cells were shaken down after the fight*.

shake off.verb type: action — dynamic; getting something to let go of you, and it takes the progressive: *he's still shaking off the flu*.
shake off.passive: **restricted** — the active is strongly preferred; the passive is possible with a pursuer, *the defender was shaken off at the top of the key*, but stilted with an illness: ✗ *this cough can't be shaken off*.

shake on.verb type: action — dynamic; a single ceremonial act, and the object is always *it*: *we agreed on a price and shook on it*.
shake on.passive: **no** — the fixed *it* leaves nothing to promote and the prepositional passive fails: ✗ *it was shaken on*, ✗ *the deal was shaken on*.

shake out.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; sense 2 (*how things shake out*) describes an outcome settling into place and is usually future-looking: *let's see how the schedule shakes out*.
shake out.passive: **restricted** — the literal sense passivizes: *the rug was shaken out on the porch*. Sense 2 takes no object and has no passive: ✗ *the schedule was shaken out*.

shake up.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; in sense 1 the participle has hardened into an adjective of state — *he was pretty shaken up* describes how he was, not what was done to him.
shake up.passive: **yes**, and sense 1 is normally passive — *she was shaken up by the crash*; *the whole front office was shaken up by the new owner*.

shine through.verb type: action in form, but it reports a persisting quality rather than an event — closest to **stative** in feel, though the progressive is fine: *her enthusiasm is shining through*.
shine through.passive: **no** — intransitive in its ordinary use, and where a noun follows, *through* is a preposition that will not passivize: ✗ *the mix was shone through by her voice*.

shoot down.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: destroying an aircraft, and rejecting an idea flatly.
shoot down.passive: **yes** — *two helicopters were shot down that night*; *every proposal I made was shot down by the committee*.

shoot for.verb type: action — dynamic; aiming at a target, and comfortable in the progressive: *we're shooting for a June launch*.
shoot for.passive: **no** — the prepositional passive is not available: ✗ *a June launch is being shot for*, ✗ *twenty pages a week were shot for*.

shoot up.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: rising sharply, growing fast, riddling a place with bullets, injecting a drug.
shoot up.passive: **restricted** — only sense 3 has one, and it is common: *the storefront was shot up and never repaired*. Senses 1, 2, and 4 take no object: ✗ *prices were shot up after the storm*.

show around.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: walking someone through a place and pointing things out. Progressive is normal — *he's showing the new hires around*.
show around.passive: **yes** — *the new hires were shown around on Monday*; *she was never shown around, so she found the break room by smell*.

show in.verb type: action — dynamic: a single act of bringing a visitor into the room. Progressive is fine — *the nurse is showing the next patient in*.
show in.passive: **yes** — *we were shown in and the door closed behind us*; *she was shown in through the side entrance*.

show off.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: behaving loudly for attention (*he's only showing off*) and displaying something proudly (*she showed off her ring*). No stative or linking use.
show off.passive: **restricted** — the display sense passivizes: *the ring was shown off at every table*. The attention-seeking sense has no object at all: ✗ *was shown off by him*.

show out.verb type: action — dynamic: walking a visitor to the door. Progressive is normal — *she's showing them out now*.
show out.passive: **yes**, and the entry uses it — *he was shown out before he could finish the sentence*; *the reporters were shown out through the lobby*.

show up.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: arriving (*he showed up two hours late*), becoming visible (*the crack showed up on the scan*), and outshining someone (*the intern showed us up*). Progressive is fine — *nobody's showing up on time*.
show up.passive: **restricted** — only the outshine sense has an object: *the whole panel was shown up by one honest answer*. The arrive and become-visible senses are objectless: ✗ *the meeting was shown up to*.

shut away.verb type: action — dynamic: putting a person or a thing somewhere closed off. Progressive is normal — *he's been shutting himself away for a week*.
shut away.passive: **yes**, and it is common — *she was shut away in a hospital for months*; *the dog gets shut away when guests come*.

shut down.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: closing a plant, powering a system off, and stopping someone cold. The machine sense is also ergative — the system can shut down on its own with no agent named.
shut down.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the mill was shut down in 1994*; *he was shut down with one question*. No passive of the intransitive *the reactor shut down automatically*.

shut off.verb type: action — dynamic: stopping a flow or a machine, or cutting someone off from contact. Progressive is normal — *they're shutting the water off at noon*.
shut off.passive: **yes**, and the second sense lives in it — *the gas was shut off at the street*; *the valley is shut off by snow for months at a time*.

shut out.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: keeping something or someone out (*heavy curtains shut out the light*) and holding an opponent scoreless (*he shut out the Sox*).
shut out.passive: **yes** — *he was shut out of the decision entirely*; *the Sox were shut out for eight innings*.

shut up.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: stopping talking, making someone stop, and closing a building for the season. No stative use.
shut up.passive: **restricted** — the two transitive senses passivize, the building one comfortably: *the cabin gets shut up every October*; *he was shut up for the rest of the meeting* is possible but stiff. The command *shut up and listen* has no object and no passive.

sing along.verb type: action — dynamic: joining in with music already playing. Progressive is normal — *half the theater was singing along*.
sing along.passive: **no** — it takes no object; what you sing along to sits behind *with* or *to*, and that will not promote: ✗ *the chorus was sung along with*.

sing out.verb type: action — dynamic: calling out loudly. Almost always objectless, and the rare object (*sang out a warning*) is still a plain act.
sing out.passive: **no** in ordinary use — the objectless use has nothing to promote, and the rare object resists: ✗ *a warning was sung out by him*. Keep it active.

sink in.verb type: action — dynamic, but a process rather than a deed: meaning arriving late (*it took a week to sink in*) or liquid soaking into a surface. Progressive is normal — *it's starting to sink in*.
sink in.passive: **no** — intransitive in both senses, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *the news was sunk in*.

sink into.verb type: action — dynamic: settling into something soft, drifting into a bad state, or pouring money in. The middle sense is a gradual change of state, not a state: *the town was sinking into a long decline*.
sink into.passive: **restricted** — only the money sense has a promotable object: *a fortune was sunk into that restaurant*. The settle and drift senses give nothing: ✗ *the armchair was sunk into*, ✗ *a depression was sunk into*.

sit around.verb type: action — dynamic, even though the activity is doing nothing; the progressive is where it lives: *we were sitting around all afternoon*.
sit around.passive: **no** — intransitive, with no object anywhere: ✗ *the shop is sat around by him*.

sit back.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: leaning back to relax, and standing by while something happens. Progressive is normal — *you're just sitting back and letting it happen*.
sit back.passive: **no** — intransitive; there is nothing to promote: ✗ *it was sat back and watched*.

sit in.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: attending as an observer, occupying a place in protest, and guesting with a band. Progressive is normal — *a lawyer was sitting in while they took the statement*.
sit in.passive: **no** — objectless; what you attend follows *on*, which is the separate [sit in on]: ✗ *the meeting was sat in*.

sit in for.verb type: action — dynamic: temporarily taking someone's place. Progressive is the usual tense — *she's sitting in for the regular host this week*.
sit in for.passive: **no** in practice — the three-part passive is not idiomatic here: ✗ *the mayor was sat in for by a deputy*. American usage keeps it active, or switches to *stand in for*.

sit in on.verb type: action — dynamic: attending a class or a meeting as an observer. Progressive is fine — *a translator is sitting in on every session*.
sit in on.passive: **restricted** — the three-part passive is marginal at best: ?*every session was sat in on by a translator*. All five entry examples are active, and that is the safe form.

sit on.verb type: action — dynamic in the delay and suppress senses (*they've been sitting on my application for a month*). The committee sense is close to **stative** — a standing position rather than an act: *she sits on the zoning board*.
sit on.passive: **yes** in the delay and suppress senses, and the entry uses it — *the story got sat on before it ever ran*; *my application has been sat on for a month*. Not in the membership sense: ✗ *the zoning board is sat on by her*.

sit out.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: skipping a round or a game, and waiting somewhere until something passes. Progressive is normal — *he's sitting out the second half*.
sit out.passive: **restricted** — possible but stilted, and rare in speech: ?*the whole election was sat out*, ?*the storm was sat out in the basement*. American usage keeps this one active.

sit through.verb type: action — dynamic: enduring something long to the end. Progressive works — *we were sitting through the fourth hour of speeches*.
sit through.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive is grammatical but stiff: ?*four hours of speeches were sat through*. It is commonest with a modal — *that video has to be sat through twice*.

sit up.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: raising yourself to sitting, staying up late, and the fixed *sit up and take notice*. Progressive is fine for the second — *she was sitting up half the night grading papers*.
sit up.passive: **no** — every sense is objectless, and the idiom is fixed and active: ✗ *notice was sat up and taken*.

sleep around.verb type: action — dynamic and habitual: the progressive is normal in the gossip it lives in — *who has been sleeping around with whom*.
sleep around.passive: **no** — intransitive; the partner is not an object here: ✗ *half the office was slept around*.

sleep in.verb type: action — dynamic: staying in bed later on purpose. Progressive works — *the kids are sleeping in for once*.
sleep in.passive: **no** — intransitive, with no object at all: ✗ *Saturday was slept in*.

sleep off.verb type: action — dynamic: getting rid of drink, jet lag, or exhaustion by sleeping. Progressive is the usual form — *he's upstairs sleeping it off*.
sleep off.passive: **restricted** — the object is nearly always *it*, and the passive is rare and clumsy: ?*the jet lag was slept off in one afternoon*. Keep it active.

sleep on.verb type: action — dynamic: deliberately putting a decision off overnight. Progressive is unusual because the act is a single decision — *I'll sleep on it* rather than ?*I'm sleeping on it*.
sleep on.passive: **yes**, and the entry ends on one — *every big decision in that family gets slept on first*; *the offer was slept on and answered in the morning*.

sleep over.verb type: action — dynamic: spending the night at someone else's house. Progressive is fine — *four kids are sleeping over on Friday*.
sleep over.passive: **no** — intransitive; the house is not an object: ✗ *his cousin's was slept over*.

sleep through.verb type: action — dynamic, though what it reports is a failure to wake: *the baby finally slept through the night*.
sleep through.passive: **restricted** — marginal and rare: ?*the alarm was slept through again*. The five entry examples are all active, and that is the natural form.

sleep with.verb type: action — dynamic: the standard American euphemism for having sex with someone. Progressive is normal — *she's not sleeping with anyone at the office*.
sleep with.passive: **no** — the prepositional passive is not idiomatic: ✗ *her best friend was slept with by him*. Reverse the subjects instead.

speak for.verb type: action — dynamic in the on-behalf sense (*she's speaking for the family tonight*). The two fixed phrases are **stative**: *his record speaks for itself* and *be spoken for* report a standing state, not an act — ✗ *that chair is being spoken for*.
speak for.passive: **restricted** — the only live passive is the fixed *be spoken for*, and it has its own meaning: *the last two puppies are already spoken for*. That blocks the literal one — *the family is spoken for by her* reads as 'claimed', not 'represented'.

speak out.verb type: action — dynamic: saying in public what you think, usually against something. Progressive is normal — *more people are speaking out now*.
speak out.passive: **no** — intransitive; what you oppose follows *against* and will not promote: ✗ *the layoffs were spoken out against by him* is not usable American English.

speak to.verb type: action — dynamic in the address-a-topic sense (*can you speak to the safety question?*) and the reprimand sense (*I'll speak to him about the noise*). The resonate sense is closer to **stative** — *that music speaks to a lot of people* — though the progressive is heard: *this song is really speaking to me*.
speak to.passive: **restricted** — the reprimand sense passivizes freely: *he was spoken to about the noise*. The topic sense is marginal (?*the safety question was never spoken to*) and the resonate sense refuses: ✗ *I was spoken to by the book*.

speak up.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: talking louder and saying the thing that needs saying. Progressive is fine — *nobody was speaking up*.
speak up.passive: **no** — intransitive, with no object in either sense: ✗ *the problem was spoken up*.

speak up for.verb type: action — dynamic: publicly backing a person or a proposal. Progressive works — *he was speaking up for her before anyone else would*.
speak up for.passive: **restricted** — the three-part passive is grammatical but stiff: ?*he was spoken up for at the hearing*. American usage prefers the active, or *be stood up for*.

speed up.verb type: action — dynamic, and ergative: the same event either way — *the line sped up* (no agent) or *new software sped up the review* (agent named).
speed up.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *the whole review was sped up by new software*; *the process has been sped up considerably*. No passive of the intransitive *the car sped up*.

spin off.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: separating part of a company, and producing a derivative show. The television sense also runs agentlessly — *a whole podcast spun off from one episode*.
spin off.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense, and the entry uses it — *two labs were spun off and later merged*; *the chemicals unit was spun off into a company of its own*. No passive of the intransitive *a podcast spun off from one episode*.

spin out.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: losing control of a car (no agent, no object) and stretching something out too long (*he spun out the story for twenty minutes*).
spin out.passive: **restricted** — only the prolong sense passivizes: *the negotiation was spun out until the deadline*. The driving sense is objectless: ✗ *the truck was spun out on black ice*.

split off.verb type: action — dynamic, and ergative: the group separates itself (*a faction split off*) or somebody separates a piece (*they split the shipping business off*).
split off.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *the shipping business was split off last year*; *the two smallest units were split off*. No passive of *a faction split off*.

split on.verb type: action — dynamic: telling authority what someone else did. Progressive is fine — *he thought his brother was splitting on him*.
split on.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive is grammatical but rare, and British where the verb is: ?*they were split on by a neighbor*. Americans would say *they got ratted on*.

split up.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: a relationship ending (no object) and dividing something or someone into parts (*we split the class up into pairs*).
split up.passive: **yes** in the divide sense — *the work was split up before anybody started*; *the class was split up into pairs*. Not in the relationship sense: *they were split up after six years* reads as somebody else separating them, not as the couple's own breakup.

spread out.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: people moving apart (no object), opening something out flat, and distributing payments over time.
spread out.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the map was spread out on the hood of the truck*; *the payments can be spread out over a year*. No passive of the disperse sense: ✗ *the riverbank was spread out along*.

spring for.verb type: action — dynamic: paying for something as a treat. A single act, so the progressive is unusual — *I'll spring for dinner* rather than ?*I'm springing for dinner*.
spring for.passive: **no** — the prepositional passive is not idiomatic: ✗ *dinner was sprung for by him*, ✗ *the good seats were sprung for*. Keep it active.

spring on.verb type: action — dynamic, and punctual: a single unannounced act. Progressive fine for the scheduled kind: *they're springing a new policy on us Monday*.
spring on.passive: **yes**, on the thing sprung, and common in the *-ing* form: *a surprise inspection was sprung on the whole department*, *nobody likes having a deadline sprung on them*. The person after *on* cannot become subject: ✗ *she was sprung the news on*.

spring up.verb type: action — dynamic, an event of sudden appearance, usually in numbers. Progressive normal: *coffee shops are springing up all over the neighborhood*.
spring up.passive: **no.** Intransitive — there is no object to promote: ✗ *tents were sprung up in the park*. For an agent, switch verbs: *they pitched tents in the park overnight*.

stand around.verb type: action — dynamic, an activity verb of idling; the progressive is its home tense: *twenty people were standing around waiting*.
stand around.passive: **no.** Intransitive: ✗ *the door was stood around by twenty people*. Any place phrase (*stood around the grill*) is an adjunct, not an object.

stand aside.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the physical stepping out of the way (*the crowd stood aside*) and the figurative giving up of a post (*he stood aside and let his deputy run it*).
stand aside.passive: **no.** Intransitive in both senses: ✗ *the stretcher was stood aside for*. The deputy sense needs a different verb for a passive: *the campaign was handed to his deputy*.

stand back.verb type: action — dynamic in the literal sense (*everyone stood back when the truck started rolling*) and in the detached-view sense, where it is a deliberate mental act: *stand back and look at the whole page*.
stand back.passive: **no.** Intransitive in both senses: ✗ *the truck was stood back from*. Say *the crowd was moved back* if you need an agent.

stand by.verb type: **stative** in the loyalty sense — a continuing stance, not an act: *I stand by every word of it*, and the progressive is odd for a statement (?*I'm standing by my estimate*) though normal of a person (*she was standing by him through all of it*). **Action — dynamic** in the readiness sense (*crews are standing by*) and the do-nothing reproach (*we can't just stand by and watch*).
stand by.passive: **no.** The loyalty sense is a prepositional verb that refuses promotion: ✗ *he was stood by by his friends*; senses 2 and 3 take no object at all: ✗ *an announcement was stood by for*.

stand down.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the resigning or backing off (*he stood down as chairman in June*) and the coming off alert (*the unit stood down at midnight*).
stand down.passive: **restricted.** No passive from ordinary intransitive use: ✗ *the chairmanship was stood down*. Only the rare military transitive gives one — *the crews were stood down once the fire was contained* — and even that is reporters' and briefers' English.

stand for.verb type: **stative** in the core senses — being an abbreviation of (*the R stands for Rachel*) and representing a principle (*it isn't clear what the party stands for*); both reject the progressive: ✗ *NPR is standing for something*. The tolerate sense is stative too, and negative-only: *I won't stand for it*, ✗ *I stand for it*. Only the British run-for-office sense is dynamic: *she's standing for Parliament in the spring*.
stand for.passive: **no.** Stative and prepositional: ✗ *Rachel is stood for by the R*, ✗ *something is stood for by the flag*. The tolerate sense is marginally attested in stiff writing (*that kind of talk will not be stood for here*), but no American says it.

stand in.verb type: action — dynamic, a temporary activity; the progressive is normal and often the point: *he's only standing in until they hire somebody*.
stand in.passive: **no.** Intransitive — the person replaced follows *for*, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *she was stood in while she was away*.

stand in for.verb type: action — dynamic, whether of a person covering a shift (*I'm standing in for Dana this week*) or a thing standing symbolically for another (*the number stands in for a name*), where it edges toward stative.
stand in for.passive: **no.** A three-part verb whose object stays put: ✗ *Dana was stood in for by me*, ✗ *the actor was stood in for by a cardboard cutout*. Say *a cutout replaced the actor*.

stand out.verb type: **stative** in both senses — being conspicuous (*a red door stands out on that street*) and being clearly better (*two applicants stood out*). It resists the progressive: ✗ *a red door is standing out on that street*; the office-speak *what's standing out to me* is the exception, not the rule.
stand out.passive: **no.** Intransitive, and stative besides: ✗ *a room full of dark suits was stood out in*. Use *set apart* for an agent: *the writing sets the album apart*.

stand up.verb type: action — dynamic in the rise sense (*everyone stood up when she came in*) and the jilting sense (*he stood her up twice*). The survive-scrutiny sense is **stative**, a disposition rather than an event: *that story won't stand up in court*, ✗ *the fabric is standing up to a lot of washing*.
stand up.passive: **yes** in the jilting sense only, and *get* is as common as *be*: *I got stood up at a very nice restaurant*. The other two senses are intransitive: ✗ *court was stood up in by that story*.

stand up for.verb type: action — dynamic, an act of open defense, usually costly and usually at a moment you can point to: *she stood up for the new guy when nobody else would*.
stand up for.passive: **no.** The three-part verb will not promote its object, and the string collides with the jilting sense of *stand up*: ✗ *the new guy was stood up for by her* reads wrong twice over. Say *she defended him*.

stand up to.verb type: action — dynamic in the confrontation sense (*she was the first person there to stand up to him*); **stative** in the withstand sense, which states a property of the thing: *these boots stand up to a New England winter*, ✗ *cheap paint is standing up to sun*.
stand up to.passive: **no.** Neither sense promotes its object: ✗ *he was stood up to by her*, ✗ *a New England winter is stood up to by these boots*. Use *withstand* — *the flood was withstood by the old bridge* — or better, keep it active.

steal away.verb type: action — dynamic, a quiet act of leaving (*they stole away before the speeches started*) or, transitively, of drawing someone off (*she stole him away from the conversation*).
steal away.passive: **restricted.** Only the transitive use passivizes, and it stays literary: *the crowd was stolen away from the main stage*. The ordinary reflexive use has no passive: ✗ *the party was stolen away from by him*, and *he was stolen away* invites the kidnapping reading.

steal up on.verb type: action — dynamic, of hunters and of time alike: *he stole up on the deer from downwind*, *winter steals up on you out here*. Progressive fine: *don't look now, but forty is stealing up on him*.
steal up on.passive: **no.** A three-part verb that will not promote its object, and the participle drags in the theft sense: ✗ *the deer was stolen up on*. Say *he crept up on the deer*.

stick around.verb type: action — dynamic, an activity of staying put; common as a bare imperative and in the progressive: *stick around*, *he's sticking around for another year*.
stick around.passive: **no.** Intransitive: ✗ *the show was stuck around after*. Time and purpose phrases (*stick around for a second year*) are adjuncts, not objects.

stick at.verb type: action — dynamic, an activity of persisting over time; British. Progressive normal: *she's sticking at it another term*.
stick at.passive: **no.** A prepositional verb whose object stays after the preposition, and *stuck* pulls in the 'jammed' reading: ✗ *the piano was stuck at for six years*. American English sidesteps it entirely with *stick with* or *keep at*.

stick by.verb type: action — dynamic, though it names a stance held over time rather than a single act: *his friends stuck by him*, *they're sticking by the plan even after the money ran out*.
stick by.passive: **no.** The object never leaves the preposition, and the passive would be read as glue or as being trapped: ✗ *he was stuck by his friends*. Say *his friends supported him*.

stick out.verb type: action — dynamic when you push something out (*don't stick your elbow out the window*) and when you endure to the end (*I'm going to stick it out*). The intransitive protrude sense is a **state** of position, though the progressive is normal for it: *a nail was sticking out of the board*. The conspicuous sense is **stative**: *he sticks out like a sore thumb*.
stick out.passive: **no** in practice. The protrude sense is intransitive; the transitive uses give bad passives that collide with *stuck* 'jammed': ✗ *her tongue was stuck out*, ✗ *the whole season was stuck out on a bad knee*.

stick to.verb type: action — dynamic, an ongoing choice not to stray: *stick to the plan*, *I'm sticking to water tonight*, *he sticks to the speed limit*.
stick to.passive: **restricted.** Formal writing allows it — *the timetable was stuck to throughout* — but the glue reading makes speakers avoid it, and ✗ *her guns were stuck to* is impossible because the object is part of a fixed phrase.

stick together.verb type: action — dynamic, a group activity sustained over time: *families stick together*, *that crew stuck together for thirty years*.
stick together.passive: **no.** Intransitive with a plural or collective subject: ✗ *they were stuck together by the crew* would say the glue thing instead.

stick up.verb type: action — dynamic in the put-up sense (*stick the notice up by the door*) and the robbery sense (*two men stuck up the liquor store*). The protrude sense is a **state** of position, though the progressive is fine: *his hair is sticking up again*.
stick up.passive: **yes** in the two transitive senses: *the notice was stuck up by the door*, *the liquor store on Tenth was stuck up by two men* — the robbery passive sounds as dated as the active. **No** passive from the protrude sense: ✗ *the ice was stuck up through*.

stick up for.verb type: action — dynamic, an act of defending someone under fire: *her brother always stuck up for her*, *somebody has to stick up for the kid*.
stick up for.passive: **no.** Three-part verbs do not promote their objects, and *stuck* misreads: ✗ *the kid was stuck up for by somebody*. Say *somebody defended the kid*.

stick with.verb type: action — dynamic in the persist and stay-close senses (*stick with it*, *stick with me and you won't get lost*). The memory sense is **stative** — the thing remembered is the subject and simply stays there: *that image stuck with me for years*.
stick with.passive: **no.** The object stays after the preposition: ✗ *the old system was stuck with for another year*. Note that *be stuck with* does exist — *I'm stuck with the bill* — but that is a different verb meaning 'be saddled with', not the passive of this one.

strike back.verb type: action — dynamic, a retaliatory event: *they struck back within the week*, *the company struck back with a lawsuit*.
strike back.passive: **no.** Intransitive — whoever you hit back at follows *at*: ✗ *he was struck back*, which would only be heard as the plain verb *strike*.

strike down.verb type: action — dynamic and punctual in both senses, the legal invalidating (*the court struck down the statute*) and the sudden felling by illness (*the epidemic struck down thousands in a month*).
strike down.passive: **yes**, and it is the usual form in both senses: *the statute was struck down on free-speech grounds*, *he was struck down by a stroke at fifty-one*.

strike off.verb type: action — dynamic and punctual, an administrative act ending a career: *the board struck her off after the second complaint*. British; an American license is *revoked*.
strike off.passive: **yes**, and it is the default: *he was struck off in 2011*, *two surgeons were struck off that year*. The *-ing* form is just as common: *being struck off ends the career, not just the job*.

strike on.verb type: action — dynamic and punctual: the moment an idea arrives, not a process. ✗ *she is striking on the answer*. Rare and literary; Americans say *hit on*.
strike on.passive: **no.** A prepositional verb whose object will not move: ✗ *the answer was struck on in the shower*, ✗ *it had not been struck on before*.

strike out.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: crossing out words (*strike out the last sentence*), the baseball event either way (*he struck out three times*; *the rookie struck him out*), failing (*I struck out with that client*), and setting off alone (*she struck out on her own at nineteen*).
strike out.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses: *the last sentence was struck out*, *the whole paragraph was struck out without asking*, *he was struck out on four pitches*. **No** passive from the batter's, the failing, or the setting-off senses, which take no object: ✗ *that client was struck out with*.

strike up.verb type: action — dynamic and inceptive: it names the beginning of a conversation, a friendship, or a piece of music, not its continuation. *They struck up a conversation in line at the post office.*
strike up.passive: **yes**, though usually without a *by*-phrase: *a friendship was struck up between them that lasted forty years*, *a march was struck up and everyone stood*.

swear at.verb type: action — dynamic, an activity that can go on: *she swore at the printer for a solid minute*, *he's swearing at the umpire again*.
swear at.passive: **yes** — one of the prepositional verbs that passivizes cleanly, especially with *get* and in the *-ing* form: *the umpire was sworn at from the stands*, *nobody likes getting sworn at*.

swear by.verb type: **stative** in the everyday faith sense — a settled belief, not an act: *my grandmother swore by cod liver oil*, ✗ *she is swearing by cod liver oil*. The older oath sense is **action — dynamic**: *he swore by everything he had that he was home that night*.
swear by.passive: **no.** Stative and prepositional at once: ✗ *cod liver oil was sworn by by my grandmother*, ✗ *that brand of tires is sworn by*. Say *she swore by it* or *she trusted it completely*.

swear in.verb type: action — dynamic and punctual, a ceremonial act performed on someone: *the clerk swore her in before a word of testimony*.
swear in.passive: **yes**, and it is the commoner form: *the mayor was sworn in on Monday morning*, *two witnesses were sworn in and then sent back out into the hall*. *Get* works too: *he gets sworn in at noon*.

swear off.verb type: action — dynamic and punctual: the moment of renouncing, not the abstaining that follows. *He swore off cigarettes in January*; the perfect carries the result: *she's sworn off dating coworkers*.
swear off.passive: **no.** The thing renounced will not become subject: ✗ *cigarettes were sworn off by him*, ✗ *sugar is sworn off every February*. Keep it active, or say *he gave up cigarettes*.

swear to.verb type: action — dynamic, an act of vouching; most often under a modal in the hedge *I couldn't swear to it*, where it names an ability rather than an event.
swear to.passive: **restricted.** Alive only in legal boilerplate — *subscribed and sworn to before me this day*, *the affidavit was sworn to in open court*. Outside that, no: ✗ *the exact time couldn't be sworn to*.

sweep aside.verb type: action — dynamic and dismissive: a single motion, literal or figurative. *He swept aside every objection anyone raised.*
sweep aside.passive: **yes** and natural: *the procedural arguments were swept aside*, *the question was swept aside and she kept talking*.

sweep away.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses — the physical carrying off (*the flood swept away the bridge*), the wholesale abolishing (*the new law swept away sixty years of rules*), and the overwhelming by feeling.
sweep away.passive: **yes**, and the third sense exists in the passive only: *the bridge was swept away by the flood*, *the old system was swept away in a single season*, *she was swept away by the whole thing and agreed on the spot*.

sweep up.verb type: action — dynamic: cleaning (*he swept the shop up after closing*), gathering fast (*she swept the papers up and left*), or being caught up in something bigger.
sweep up.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses, and the third is passive-only: *the glass was swept up before anybody stepped in it*, *they got swept up in the excitement and bought two*. **No** passive from the objectless use: ✗ *it was swept up by me* for *I'll sweep up*.

swing at.verb type: action — dynamic and punctual — an attempt, not a hit: *he swung at me and missed by a foot*, *she swung at the first pitch*.
swing at.passive: **restricted.** Possible with a human object in casual speech — *I've been swung at plenty of times* — but flat with a thing: ✗ *the first pitch was swung at by her*, ✗ *the piñata was swung at*.

swing by.verb type: action — dynamic, a brief detour on the way somewhere else; American and informal. *I'll swing by the store on the way home*, *swing by around six*.
swing by.passive: **no.** The place after *by* is a destination, not a promotable object: ✗ *the store was swung by on the way home*, ✗ *the office was swung by to drop off the keys*.
